notes.meaning: Eliphaz breaks the week-long silence to respond to Job's bitter complaint. He came from Teman, an area famous throughout the ancient world for wise thinkers. Even though he speaks with an outward show of politeness, he assumes Job's terrible suffering must be the punishment for some sin.

Eliphaz asks politely whether Job can bear to hear a word from his friends, or if it will only make him more weary. Even though he knows his words might hurt, Eliphaz feels he cannot hold his tongue any longer. In his mind, God's justice has been questioned and must be defended.

Eliphaz recalls how helpful Job had been to other hurting people during his days of prosperity. Job had often stepped in to teach the discouraged, steadying hands that hung down in despair and bracing knees that were giving way under pressure. He was known as a gentle and wise helper to those carrying great trials.

Now that hardship has fallen on Job himself, Eliphaz points out that Job has collapsed into despair. It is always far easier to preach patience to someone else than to practice it when pain touches our own lives. Eliphaz treats Job's deep grief as a failure of character rather than showing tender sympathy.

Eliphaz asks Job whether his reverence for God and his upright life are truly giving him any confidence right now. He argues that if Job's faith were genuine, he would not be so completely undone by his troubles. He begins to imply that Job's past godliness may have been an empty show.

Eliphaz challenges Job to name a single time when an innocent or upright person was permanently destroyed by God. He assumes that God shields good people from total ruin, which leads him to suspect that Job is guilty of secret sins. In reality, godly people often suffer deeply in this world, just as righteous Abel did at the beginning.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some modern prosperity teachers teach a similar view, claiming that real faith always guarantees physical health and wealth, and that severe suffering must come from personal sin or lack of faith.

notes.meaning: Eliphaz appeals to his own life experience, comparing moral choices to planting and harvesting a field. Those who plow the soil for wickedness and scatter seeds of trouble will surely reap a harvest of ruin. While this principle often holds true, Eliphaz misapplies it by treating it as a rule with no exceptions.

God can destroy the wicked instantly with nothing more than a breath of His mouth. Eliphaz draws an image from the scorching desert winds that wither and blast living plants in moments. He may also be making a harsh reference to the sudden windstorm that collapsed the house on Job's children.

Eliphaz pictures fierce, roaring lions whose teeth are suddenly shattered, leaving them to starve while their cubs are scattered. In the ancient world, lions symbolized ruthless rulers and powerful bullies who preyed upon the helpless. Eliphaz hints that Job was like one of these tyrants whose ill-gotten wealth and family have now been wiped out by God.

To give his counsel divine authority, Eliphaz recounts a mysterious message that came secretly to him. He caught only a quiet whisper of it, emphasizing how holy and rare the experience was. Before the Scriptures were written down, God often revealed His truth to people through such private revelations.

The message arrived during the dead of night while other men were locked in deep, trance-like sleep. Eliphaz had removed himself from the busy daytime world and was meditating in the quiet darkness when these visions began. A still and quiet heart was a fitting place to receive a message from the spiritual world.

Before he even saw or heard anything, an overwhelming dread gripped Eliphaz, making every bone in his body tremble. When fallen human beings brush against the supernatural realm, their natural reaction is awe and terror. God often humbles a person in this way before delivering a solemn truth.

A spiritual presence glided right past his face, chilling him so deeply that the hair all over his skin stood on end. The experience was terrifying and uncanny, completely shaking his composure. The apparition made a deep and fearful impression on him.

differ.view: Some evangelicals believe this spirit was an evil angel or demon, noting that it brought darkness and tormenting fear rather than the peaceful assurance usually brought by God's holy angels.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern scholars translate the word as a sudden breath of wind or gust of air that passed over his face and made his hair stand up.

notes.meaning: The figure stopped and stood still right before his eyes, but its shape was too shadowy and indistinct to make out. After a tense and total silence, a calm, whispering voice spoke to him out of the quiet. The mysterious form kept Eliphaz focused on the words being spoken rather than on the messenger.

The voice asked whether any mortal human can ever claim to be more righteous or pure than God his Maker. No frail person can justify themselves before the Almighty or accuse Him of treating them unfairly. Whenever someone grumbles against God's providence, they are acting as if their own sense of right and wrong is superior to His.

Even the heavenly angels are mere servants who fall infinitely short of God's uncreated perfection. If God does not place absolute trust even in heavenly beings, frail mortals on earth have no right to boast of their own righteousness.

differ.view: Methodists have often understood this as a direct reference to the fallen angels, who rebelled against God in their folly and lost their original place.
Reformed writers generally teach that this refers to holy angels, showing that even the highest created spirits have limits and are imperfect when measured against God's absolute holiness.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic commentary has traditionally followed the early church fathers in applying this verse to the historical rebellion and fall of the angels.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Modern scholars note that ancient wisdom literature often viewed all created heavenly beings as naturally fallible before God, without drawing a sharp line between good and fallen angels.

notes.meaning: Human beings are far weaker than heavenly angels because their souls live in fragile bodies made of clay. People were formed from the dirt and rest on an unstable foundation of dust. They are so delicate that they can be crushed just as easily as a common moth between two fingers.

From sunrise to sunset, mortals are constantly wasting away and breaking down toward the grave. Life is as brief as a single day, and when people perish, they vanish from this earthly life forever. Death happens so often and so quietly that the rest of the world barely stops to pay attention.

Death snaps the cords of a person's life just like tearing down a nomad's tent. Human advantages like beauty, wealth, and strength disappear the moment the body collapses into dust. Tragically, many people die without ever acquiring the true spiritual wisdom that prepares a soul for eternity.
